The inverse design method prescribes desired distributions of angle of attack (α) and axial induction factor (a) along the blade span.
The RANS/ADM CFD model is used to compute the aerodynamic performance of the blade geometry during the inverse design iterations.
The Trust-Region-Reflective optimization method is used to update the blade geometry (twist and chord distributions) to match the desired α and a targets.
The inverse design method is demonstrated for both conventional single-rotor wind turbines and dual-rotor wind turbines (DRWTs).
Manufacturing and transportation constraints on conventional turbine blades lead to aerodynamically suboptimal designs in the blade root region.
The DRWT configuration uses a secondary smaller rotor in front of the main rotor to more efficiently extract energy from the blade root region.
The DRWT can also enhance flow entrainment and wake mixing, leading to reduced wake losses compared to a conventional single-rotor design.
The inverse design method is general and can be applied to wind turbines with an arbitrary number of rotor disks, not just DRWTs.
A mesh sensitivity study showed that a grid resolution of 101x229 cells was sufficient to obtain grid-independent results for the RANS/ADM solver.
The Trust-Region-Reflective method was found to be more stable than the multi-dimensional Newton iteration method when there are constraints on the blade design.
The multi-dimensional Newton method converged faster than the Trust-Region-Reflective method for unconstrained blade optimization problems.
The inverse design algorithm was able to reproduce the original blade geometry of the NREL 5 MW wind turbine with less than 1% error.
The inverse design approach allows the designer to directly specify the desired aerodynamic performance targets (α and a distributions) and obtain the corresponding blade geometry.
The RANS/ADM model used in this study has been previously validated against experimental data for wind turbine aerodynamic performance prediction.
The inverse design methodology presented in this paper is general and can be applied to a wide range of wind turbine configurations, not just single-rotor and dual-rotor designs.
